prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought the measurement of time to a new level of precision

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as a stand-alone prize to Katori and Ye, the same configuration as in round 1. In round 1 I moved to it from IceCube, and I have tested that move against the whole exchange and the chair's questions. My one-sentence answer to the chair's first question is this: the 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb, which counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize honoured quantum control of single trapped ions, whereas the lattice clock is a different invention, trapping thousands of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the trap does not shift the clock transition, which brings both stability and accuracy to the 1e-18 level. That is a measurement result that has been reproduced and intercompared by independent laboratories (RIKEN and Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, NPL), and it has already given physics: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tighter limits on drifting constants, ultralight dark-matter searches and many-body clocks. As an experimentalist I regard a new instrument that opens a new measurement regime and is confirmed independently as a legitimate physics achievement, not a lesser one. The credit is compact: the concept and first lattice clock are Katori's, and the record-accuracy and many-body realisation are Ye's. No member has raised a scientific objection that the physics is unsound, and six of eight now include it in their preferred configuration.
statement.case_against: Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is the strongest argument against, and a purist can still call this the next increment in optical metrology. The redefinition of the second has not been adopted, so the headline application is still prospective, although I regard that as procedure and not as a test of whether the physics works. The two-name credit leaves out Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto, and I cannot verify the Tokyo-versus-JILA priority details myself, so I rely on the external expert reports for that. Finally, I must be honest that the breadth of support is partly produced by convergence after the opening ballots (I am one of those who moved), and that the condensed-matter members rank it low or mid. I take it as a weakness that I have no independent test of the case from outside AMO beyond the arguments made in round 1. A second part would not cure these weaknesses: I do not see a second shortlisted achievement that shares a thread with the clock and that I can defend, and a prize pairing unrelated fields would be a compromise and not a judgment.

responses.point: Kroll says Katori conceived the magic-wavelength scheme and built the first strontium lattice clock, Ye's group took it to the systematic and coherence limits and developed the many-body clock, and that this makes two names the clean split despite the 2005 and 2012 precedents.
responses.response: I accept that split and I use your account in my citation. Where I still need more than the statements in this room is the early Tokyo and JILA priority. You and Lindroth are asked by the chair for draft wording, and I would like it to name the invention and the 1e-18 development together, so that Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and Lemonde are not implicitly denied. I do not support a third name, since I cannot say which of them did work that is decisive in the same way, and I would not trade a defensible pair for a weaker trio. I agree with your remark that the redefinition is a matter of procedure, not of whether the physics works.

responses.point: Danielsson pairs B040 with Hosono's iron-based superconductors (B028) as two distinct, mature, cleanly credited achievements within three names, while admitting that the pairing has no common thread and that the pairing mechanism is unexplained.
responses.response: I considered your configuration seriously, because the two-part form is allowed and Hosono's 2008 observation was confirmed within weeks and has stood for eighteen years. But I do not support a second part for two reasons. First, I cannot judge from my own field whether a family discovery whose mechanism is unexplained, and whose Tc increases came from other groups, is as decisive as the clock, and no member outside you and Olsson supports it. Second, you yourself call the pairing a compromise, and I do not want to add a part just to use the third name. If Eriksson or Mehlig, who know the field better, argue strongly for B028 as a discovery, I will listen. As things stand I keep B028 off my own configuration and not among my two alternatives, but I do not say it is a weak candidate.

responses.point: Olsson asked me in round 1 to say concretely what Karle and Halzen each did that others did not, and says attribution is the one point she will not compromise on, which is why she moved to B040 and B028.
responses.response: You were right to press me, and my answer is that I cannot show that two names capture the first detection of the astrophysical neutrino flux, since the instrument and the analyses were produced by a collaboration of hundreds, with the AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors outside the slate. Halzen's long leadership of the concept and Karle's central role in the detector are real, but that is not the same as showing that nobody else did something decisive. This is the reason I now put B018 only as my second alternative, behind B061, and not as a preferred part. On B028, I take your point that Hosono's credit is clean, but I do not follow you in making it a second part, for the reasons I gave to Danielsson.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B061 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a stand-alone prize, calls it the chain of prediction, observation and two decades of independent confirmation that he trusts most, and lists B040 as his first alternative while admitting he cannot judge priority details in atomic physics.
responses.response: Your reply to the chair's question is the most useful for me, because you say B040 is broadly supported and that you do not object on scientific grounds but from distance to the field. That is what I wanted to hear. On B061 I remain where I was: I rate it as a mature and well-confirmed achievement and keep it as my first alternative, but the credit gap for Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D pioneers is something I cannot judge for myself. Olsson, Danielsson and Mehlig, who work closer to it, read it as contestable, and Mehlig says B040 is the better-attributed fallback. If you and Mehlig can show that a citation built on the Kane-Mele prediction and the Molenkamp observation handles that gap, I would be willing to see B061 on the final ballot as a serious rival. I think the 2016 prize is a partial and not a full overlap.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clock first for originality, reproducibility and a stable two-person attribution, and herself asks for a colleague from outside AMO to test whether it reads as a fundamental result or as an instrument.
responses.response: I take your request as addressed partly to me. As an outsider to AMO, though not to measurement physics, I read the lattice clock as a fundamental result for the reason that it changed what can be measured: gravitational redshift over a millimetre, constants and dark-matter bounds that were not available before. I do not read it as only a better ruler. I would still like the citation to avoid the word 'precision' alone, and to say that the invention and its development to 1e-18 are the achievement, so that the instrument claim is made on its physics. I agree with you that the pending redefinition of the second is confirmation of maturity, not evidence that the case is prospective.

uncertainties: Whether external expert reports confirm that Katori (concept, first lattice clock) and Ye (record accuracy, many-body clocks) are decisive over Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto, since I cannot verify early Tokyo versus JILA priority myself.

Whether the committee will read the lattice clock as a distinct invention and a discovery in physics, not an increment on the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the condensed-matter members' lower rankings are scientific or only distance from the field.
Whether the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp credit gap for B061 can be handled by citation wording, which would make it a real rival, and whether B028 deserves a second part despite the unexplained mechanism.
My knowledge of clock history and of the credit chains for B061, B028 and IceCube is general and has not been checked against the literature.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict specific to the lattice clock: I work in astroparticle physics (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur), have no recorded personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the clock groups, and have none to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hosono or the IceCube leadership. Field proximity to IceCube is the only thing to disclose, and I now hold it as a second alternative, not a preferred part. As Chair I have tried not to treat the count of members who moved to B040 as a substitute for judgment.
